rv.q: The play opens up interesting ideas about mutual antagonism and dependency – between siblings, between the sexes, between outlooks – but the structure thwarts deeper exploration of them, so it feels frustrating.
I simply feel that there is something contradictory about LaBute's desire to attack our endless capacity for self-deception and his palpable delight in manipulating an audience.
This forest is dark, but it is not all that deep.
Lurking back somewhere there is their father. On the sofa, in a rare moment of repose, they share a joint and get closer.
The scintillating savagery of early LaBute plays has atrophied into cliche.
The play nevertheless works well as an intriguing psychological thriller and if you can see the final revelation coming Bobby’s reaction is less easy to predict.

cn.t: LaBute's two-hander provokes with twists and sibling antagonism, but critics find the plotting contrived and predictable. Fox and Williams deliver strong performances in a play that entertains without reaching the playwright's best work.
